analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate to 15 percent and adjusts investment gains for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in the House; it died after being referred to the Ways and Means Committee, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the tax rate on profits from selling stocks and other long-held assets from as high as 31 percent down to a 15 percent maximum, and to 7.5 percent for low- and middle-income taxpayers [S2][S3]. It would also have let sellers of corporate stock and business property increase their purchase price for tax purposes by the amount of inflation since they bought it, reducing the taxable gain [S2][S3]. Because most capital gains go to the wealthiest households, the tax cut would have flowed mainly to them, while reducing federal revenue [S2]. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never moved further; Congress adjourned without it ever getting a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell stocks and business property at a profit would pay much less tax: a top rate of 15 percent instead of the rates then in law, with indexing meaning inflation-driven gains would go untaxed [S2][S3]. Because capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, the largest dollar benefits would go to wealthy individuals and to corporations selling assets [S2]. Venture capital and other investors backing new businesses, the group the bill's title points to, would keep more of their returns [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors and corporations selling assets

how_it_helps.text: Caps the tax rate on long-term capital gains at 15 percent for individuals and corporations, down from rates as high as 31 percent for individuals and 34 percent for corporations [S2][S3].
Sets a 7.5 percent capital gains rate for the portion of gains falling within the low- and middle-income tax brackets, so smaller investors pay less too [S2][S3].

Lets owners of stock and business property held more than a year adjust their purchase price upward by inflation, using the gross national product deflator, so purely inflationary gains are not taxed [S2][S3].
Raises the $3,000 annual limit on deductible capital losses for individuals by inflation each year, a modest benefit to taxpayers with investment losses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally, would bear the cost of the lower rates and inflation adjustments through reduced federal revenue [S2]. The benefit is concentrated among households that own stocks and business assets, which are disproportionately high-income, so the tax burden would effectively shift toward people whose income comes from wages [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury and wage earners generally

drawbacks.text: Capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, so the largest tax savings would flow to the wealthiest investors, widening the gap between how wages and investment income are taxed [S2].
The rate cut and indexing would reduce federal revenue at a time of budget deficits, meaning either higher taxes elsewhere, lower spending, or more borrowing [S2].

Cutting the top rate to 15 percent while ordinary wage income faced higher rates would widen the difference in tax treatment between investment income and paychecks, creating an incentive to recharacterize income as capital gains [S2].
Indexing rules in the bill are complex, excluding many asset types and requiring the Treasury to publish quarterly inflation tables, adding compliance cost for investors and the IRS [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Small investors would get a modest benefit from the 7.5 percent rate on lower-bracket gains, but the bulk of the tax cut would go to high-income households and corporations, who hold most capital gains [S2]. Weighing that against the lost federal revenue and the deeper preference for investment income over wages, the bill's main effect would be a large tax reduction skewed toward the wealthy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Mickey Edwards of Oklahoma introduced the bill on July 11, 1991, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax law [S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy investors gained nothing, but the status quo prevailed: current tax rates on capital gains stayed in place, and the Treasury kept the revenue the cut would have cost. Ordinary taxpayers were spared the revenue loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury and the tax status quo

for.name: Rep. Mickey Edwards
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; it was referred to Ways and Means the same day.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: The House committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have cut the tax rate on stock and business-asset gains to 15 percent and exempted inflationary gains, but it died in committee, so investors kept paying the higher rates in law [S2][S3]. Because gains concentrate among the wealthy, the defeated cut would have shifted tax burden toward wage earners.

The bill's title targets venture capital; a lower 15 percent rate would have raised after-tax returns on successful startup investments [S2][S3]. With the bill dead, those returns remain taxed at the higher rates in law.

The bill would have cut the corporate capital gains rate from 34 percent to 15 percent and reduced the corporate minimum tax on gains [S2][S3]. It never advanced, so corporate sellers keep the existing rate.
